items.title: The Gulf Stream warms western Europe by an estimated 5 °C
items.claim: How much does ocean circulation warm western Europe?

options.text: Not at all — climate is determined by latitude alone

Comparison with similar-latitude locations (Calgary, Labrador) and modelling studies suggest the wider North Atlantic circulation system contributes around 5-10 °C of additional warmth to western Europe
By 30 °C — without it Europe would be like Antarctica

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream is the western boundary current of the North Atlantic gyre; it broadens north of Cape Hatteras into the North Atlantic Current. Prevailing westerlies carry the heat onshore.

Richard Seager and colleagues (2002) argued that atmospheric heat transport and the southwesterly stationary wave (set up by the Rocky Mountains) are at least as important as ocean heat in distinguishing western from eastern continental winters. The single-cause 'Gulf Stream warms Britain' story is too simple.

The AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation) has weakened by an estimated 15% since the mid-20th century (Caesar et al., 2018, 2021). A collapse would cool Europe and warm the tropics.
items.why: Climate is the product of multiple systems acting together. The Gulf Stream story is partly true and partly simplified; a teaching answer needs both the ocean and the atmosphere.

items.title: Tides are driven by both the Moon and the Sun
items.claim: What causes spring and neap tides?

options.text: The Moon provides about two-thirds of the tidal force, the Sun about one-third; when Sun, Earth and Moon align (new and full moon), tidal pulls combine for spring tides; at first/last quarter they oppose for neap tides — roughly fortnightly
Spring tides occur only in March-April
Tides are caused by Earth's rotation alone

items.reveal:
The Moon's gravity raises a tidal bulge facing it (and another on the opposite side of the Earth). The Sun does the same but with one-third the force despite being much more massive — distance scales as the cube in tidal force.

At new and full moon (syzygy — alignment), the bulges add: spring tides, with the largest tidal range. At first and last quarter (90° angle), the Sun partly cancels the Moon: neap tides, smaller range.

The Bay of Fundy (Canada) has the world's largest tidal range, around 16 m. The Bristol Channel (Avonmouth) is second at around 15 m. 'Spring' here is from Old English 'springan' (to leap), not the season.
items.why: Etymological confusion can become factual confusion. Students often think spring tides only happen in spring; the actual mechanism is gravitational alignment, fortnightly, regardless of season.

items.title: Sampling strategy affects every fieldwork result
items.claim: Why does a geographer choose a stratified sample over a random one?

options.text: Stratified sampling deliberately includes proportions from defined subgroups (e.g. age categories in a questionnaire, river sections by gradient), reducing risk of missing minority categories

items.reveal:
Sampling types: random (every member equally likely), systematic (every nth member, e.g. every 10 metres along a transect), stratified (proportional samples from defined groups), opportunistic (whoever is available — least rigorous).

At A-level, the NEA Independent Investigation requires explicit justification of sampling strategy. Small samples (n<30) limit statistical analysis; sub-group analysis needs larger samples in each stratum.

Fieldwork ethics, including consent for questionnaires and impact on study sites, has become more prominent.
items.why: Bad sampling produces bad results regardless of how impressive the spreadsheet looks. Sampling design is upstream of all subsequent analysis.
